questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) (i) List two reasons for the study of Logic.

(ii) State the difference between a Concrete Term and an Abstract Term. (2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Two reasons for the study of Logic.**
- Logic trains the mind to reason correctly: it teaches us to tell a valid argument from an invalid one.
- Logic helps us to detect and avoid fallacies, and so to express our thoughts clearly, consistently and in an orderly way.

(Other accepted reasons: it sharpens critical thinking; it helps us to evaluate the arguments of other people; it improves discussion and decision making.)

**(ii) Concrete term and abstract term.** A **concrete term** names an individual thing, person or substance that exists in its own right and can be perceived (e.g. "table", "teacher", "Douala"). An **abstract term** names a quality, attribute or state considered apart from the things that have it; it exists only in the mind as a concept (e.g. "honesty", "whiteness", "poverty"). Example: "man" is concrete, "humanity" is abstract.
themes: O Level Logic - nature and scope of logic
O Level Logic - definition and division

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) What is the difference between:

(i) A Sentence and a Proposition?

(ii) Quantity and Quality? (2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A **sentence** is a group of words arranged according to the rules of grammar that expresses a complete thought; it may be a statement, a question, a command, a wish or an exclamation, and it belongs to one language. A **proposition** is the **meaning** of a declarative sentence: what is affirmed or denied, and so what is either true or false. Only statements are propositions; questions and commands are not. Several different sentences (or sentences in different languages) can express the same proposition: "Paul loves Mary" and "Mary is loved by Paul".

**(ii)** The **quantity** of a proposition is the extent of its subject term: it is **universal** (all, no, every: the predicate is said of the whole subject) or **particular** (some: only a part of the subject). The **quality** of a proposition is the nature of the link between subject and predicate, shown by the copula: it is **affirmative** (is, are) or **negative** (is not, are not). Example: "All teachers are graduates" is universal affirmative (A); "Some teachers are not graduates" is particular negative (O).
themes: O Level Logic - propositions and their types
O Level Logic - nature and scope of logic

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) State one rule of Contrariety.

(ii) Define the Figure of the Syllogism. (2 x 2 marks)

(d) (i) When is an Enthymeme considered to be in the First Order?

(ii) Give two reasons why the study of Fallacies are important. (2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** An **enthymeme** is a syllogism with one of its three propositions left unstated (understood but not expressed). In the traditional classification an enthymeme is **of the first order when the major premise is suppressed**: only the minor premise and the conclusion are expressed. (Second order: the minor premise is suppressed; third order: the conclusion is suppressed.) Example: "Paul is a teacher; therefore Paul is a graduate" (suppressed major premise: "All teachers are graduates").

**(ii) Importance of the study of fallacies** (any two):
- It helps us to **detect errors** in the reasoning of other people (advertisers, politicians, opponents in a debate) and not to be misled by arguments that only look convincing.
- It helps us to **avoid committing fallacies** ourselves, and so to argue correctly and to defend true conclusions with sound reasons.
- It improves clarity of thought and the quality of discussion.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e) Briefly explain the following:

(i) Simple Statement.

(ii) Truth-Table. (2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A **simple statement** is a statement that asserts one single thing and does not contain any other statement as a component: it has one subject and one predicate and no logical connective joining statements. Example: "Paul is tall." It is symbolised by one variable, e.g. $p$. (A compound statement, such as "Paul is tall and Mary is short", is built from simple statements by connectives.)

**(ii)** A **truth-table** is a table that lists all the possible combinations of truth-values (T or F) of the component statements of a compound statement or an argument and shows, row by row, the resulting truth-value of the whole. With $n$ different variables the table has $2^n$ rows. Example for conjunction:

| $p$ | $q$ | $p \cdot q$ |
|---|---|---|
| T | T | T |
| T | F | F |
| F | T | F |
| F | F | F |
themes: O Level Logic - symbolic logic basics
